South Florida Presbytery Two ministers appealed Presbytery’s divestiture of their offices after their congregations left the PCA. The SJC reversed because their calls had never been formally dissolved, so they were not automatically without call, and BCO 34-10 did not apply while they remained actively engaged and accepted in ministry. The SJC could not judge their fairness and pretext claims from the record. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2025-13" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2025-13 Felipe Assis and Carter Brown v. South Florida Presbytery Two ministers appealed Presbytery’s decision to divest them of office without censure after their congregations left the PCA. The SJC sustained the BCO-violation specification and reversed the divestitures: their calls had never been formally dissolved, and BCO 34-10 did not apply because they continued performing ministerial functions and remained accepted by their churches. It declined as unable to judge claims that Presbytery disregarded their emails or used the procedure as discriminatory pretext. The ministers returned to good standing; Presbytery must dissolve their existing PCA calls and then pursue a BCO-consistent option. appeal sustained; reversed mixed legacy 2025-13 8-7 13-2 20-8 21-1 23-1 34-10 38-3.a 46-7 divestiture without censure ministerial status dissolution of pastoral call church withdrawal transfer of credentials presbytery jurisdiction"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2025-13</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga52_2025__2025-12_2025-13.md">Felipe Assis and Carter Brown v. <section class="judicial-year" data-judicial-year="2023"><h2>2023</h2><div class="judicial-year__records"><article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-05" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2023-05 Hyland v. Chicago Metro Presbytery Former church employee Emily Hyland complained to the SJC after Chicago Metro Presbytery ruled her BCO 43 complaint out of order because, as a local-church member, she was not subject to Presbytery's jurisdiction. The SJC was equally divided 12–12–0 on the proposed panel decision, so CMP's ruling stands. That proposed decision would have answered that CMP did not err: Hyland lacked standing to file a BCO 43-1 complaint with Presbytery. No amendments were made. An evenly divided SJC thus leaves the lower ruling in place without a majority rationale. complaint denied not stated legacy 2023-5 43-1 31-2 32-2 standing to complain employment termination BCO 43-1 standing church employee accusations against teaching elders judicially out of order civil authorities"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-05</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga52_2025__2023-05.md">Hyland v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-01" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2023-01 Hann v. Pee Dee Presbytery Kristin Hann's complaint against Pee Dee Presbytery was dismissed because the SJC held she lacked standing: she was not subject to Pee Dee Presbytery's jurisdiction, so the complaint was judicially out of order and could not be put in order. The SJC made no merits ruling and stated that the ruling did not stay Presbytery's continuing investigation or review of resulting actions. The adopted ruling was approved 17-2; Maynard and Sartorius dissented without stated reasons, four were absent, and Ross recused. complaint dismissed not reached legacy 2023-1 46-8 43-1 standing to complain jurisdiction of presbytery complainant not subject to presbytery jurisdiction judicially out of order"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-01</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga51_2024__2023-01.md">Hann v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-02" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2023-02 Reynolds v. Pee Dee Presbytery The SJC dismissed Mrs. Kappie Reynolds's complaint against Pee Dee Presbytery as judicially out of order. The complaint challenged a Session's reception of and action on a confession at a meeting more than six months before filing, far outside BCO 43-2's sixty-day period; the SJC held the untimeliness was not demonstrated curable. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-04" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2023-04 Biese et al. v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery Biese and others complained that Tennessee Valley Presbytery erred by approving Redeemer Church session minutes without exception—minutes noting a youth Super Bowl party—and by denying their complaint seeking a Sabbath exception. The SJC denied the complaint: because Presbytery gave no reasons for its actions, the record was insufficient to find it erred in interpreting the Constitution. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-06" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2023-06 Knox Baird et al. v. Grace Presbytery Session elders challenged Presbytery’s handling of a mediation complaint, investigative directives, BCO 40-5 reports, and a trial stay. The SJC held that the mediation complaint was never formally filed and became moot; official-record requests were proper, but compelling nonrecord personal communications and requiring the Session to address its congregation exceeded Presbytery’s authority. It vacated the communications directive and annulled the stay for lack of the required prior citation. It upheld committee examination of the BCO 40-5 reports and did not reach alleged partiality; the Session trials were to proceed. complaint partially sustained; denied; moot not stated legacy 2023-6 40-5 complaint procedure BCO 40-5 review document production stay of judicial proceedings mootness"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2023-06</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga51_2024__2023-06_2023-08.md">Knox Baird et al. v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-07" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2023-07 Evans v. Arizona Presbytery Arizona Presbytery divested a minister without censure for prolonged lack of call after he had joined an EPCEW congregation and notified Presbytery of his withdrawal. The SJC sustained his appeal and reversed the divestiture because BCO 38-3(a) had already ended Presbytery's jurisdiction while he was in good standing and under no investigation or charges. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-08" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2023-08 Knox Baird et al. v. Grace Presbytery Session elders challenged Presbytery’s handling of a withdrawn mediation complaint, document and congregational-notice directives, BCO 40-5 reports, and a stay of Session trials. The SJC sustained the complaints in the main: the mediation complaint was never formally filed and became moot; Presbytery could require official record materials but not compel personal communications or force the Session to address its congregation; and the stay lacked a prior BCO 40-5 citation. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-11" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2023-11 Psiaki v. Pacific Northwest Presbytery The SJC sustained Psiaki’s complaint and held that the CPC Session erred by ordaining and installing officers elected at a February 5, 2023 congregational meeting where the congregation’s bylaw excluded communing members under 18 from voting. Reading BCO 6-4, 25-1, and 25-7 together, the SJC ruled that all communing members are entitled to vote and that local bylaws cannot impose an age restriction; the “good and regular standing” language addresses censure, not age. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-13" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2023-13 BCO 40-5 Matter re Metropolitan NY A BCO 40-5 citation arose from Metro New York Presbytery's failure to redress a session that allowed a woman to expound Scripture in place of the sermon preceding the Lord's Supper, held services without preaching, and celebrated the Supper without a preceding sermon. The SJC remitted the matter to the presbytery for constitutional resolution because the session's later no-exception response was clearly inadequate and the unapproved minutes were unclear. Presbytery must complete its work with TE Higgins and Trinity Presbyterian Church's session and report to the 51st General Assembly. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2023-15" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2023-15 Tom Turner v. South Florida Presbytery Turner complained against Presbytery Judicial Commission actions deposing TE Tommy Boland and dissolving Cross Community Church’s relationship with Presbytery. The SJC ruled both complaints administratively out of order for lack of standing and incapable of being put in order. Cross Community had already disaffiliated through its first congregational motion; the second motion, which contemplated later implementation, was out of order as contingent. Because no Presbytery action was required to effect disaffiliation, Turner was no longer a PCA member. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-23" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2022-23 Woodham v. South Florida Presbytery South Florida Presbytery deposed a Teaching Elder, suspended him from the sacraments, and later excommunicated him without first assigning him to a particular church under BCO 46-8. The complainant argued that omission stripped Presbytery of jurisdiction. The SJC denied the complaint: BCO 46-8 requires assignment but fixes no timeframe or mechanism; a deposed minister remains under Presbytery's jurisdiction until transfer, and BCO 37-9(a) preserves censure authority. Deferring under BCO 39-3, the SJC found no clear error in Presbytery's efforts. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-04" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2022-04 Sheppard v. Highlands Presbytery The SJC sustained TE Craig Sheppard's complaint against Highlands Presbytery. It held that Presbytery erred when its Judicial Commission found a strong presumption of guilt but, instead of instituting process under BCO 31-2, directed pastoral reconciliation and conditioned later process on its success; that motion also impaired the accused's right against self-incrimination. It further held that BCO 32-20's one-year time bar had run and that the 2022 amendment did not apply retroactively, so Presbytery is debarred from prosecuting the allegations. Four commissioners dissented, disputing the BCO 32-20 ruling. complaint sustained discretion and judgment legacy 2022-4 31-2 32-20 11-3 11-4 14-3 14-7 27-1 27-2 27-3 39-3 39-3.2 39-3.3 31-3 13-2 34-10 40-5 32-20.18 timeliness of process BCO 32-20 statute of limitations strong presumption of guilt BCO 31-2 mandatory process judicial and pastoral procedures case of scandal retroactive application of BCO amendments debarment from prosecution stare decisis in ecclesiastical courts"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2022-04</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga50_2023__2022-04.md">Sheppard v. It held that Presbytery erred when its Judicial Commission found a strong presumption of guilt but, instead of instituting process under BCO 31-2, directed pastoral reconciliation and conditioned later process on its success; that motion also impaired the accused's right against self-incrimination. It further held that BCO 32-20's one-year time bar had run and that the 2022 amendment did not apply retroactively, so Presbytery is debarred from prosecuting the allegations. Four commissioners dissented, disputing the BCO 32-20 ruling.</p><div class="judicial-case__topics" aria-label="Topic tags"><span class="judicial-pill">timeliness of process</span><span class="judicial-pill">BCO 32-20 statute of limitations</span><span class="judicial-pill">strong presumption of guilt</span><span class="judicial-pill judicial-pill--more">+6 topics</span></div><div class="judicial-case__footer"><a href="../cases/ga50_2023__2022-04.md">Read case <span aria-hidden="true">→</span></a><details class="judicial-details"><summary>Case details</summary><dl><div><dt>Matter type</dt><dd>Complaint</dd></div><div><dt>Final disposition</dt><dd>Sustained</dd></div><div><dt>Review basis</dt><dd>Great deference unless clear error (discretion and judgment)</dd></div><div><dt>BCO provisions</dt><dd>BCO 31-2, BCO 32-20, BCO 11-3, BCO 11-4, BCO 14-3, BCO 14-7, BCO 27-1, BCO 27-2, BCO 27-3, BCO 39-3, BCO 39-3.2, BCO 39-3.3, BCO 31-3, BCO 13-2, BCO 34-10, BCO 40-5, BCO 32-20.18</dd></div><div><dt>Aliases</dt><dd>legacy 2022-4</dd></div><div><dt>All topic tags</dt><dd>timeliness of process, BCO 32-20 statute of limitations, strong presumption of guilt, BCO 31-2 mandatory process, judicial and pastoral procedures, case of scandal, retroactive application of BCO amendments, debarment from prosecution, stare decisis in ecclesiastical courts</dd></div></dl></details></div></article>

Northwest Georgia Presbytery The SJC declined to reach a complaint arising from judicial process against three ruling elders (not the complainants), because the Session dismissed all charges and ended that process on July 23, 2022, and the elders resigned and their calls were dissolved. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2022-01" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2022-01 Eagle v. Savannah River Presbytery The SJC dismissed Eric Eagle and others' complaint against Savannah River Presbytery as administratively out of order and untimely under BCO 43-3. The complaint was first filed prematurely in December 2020; after the SJC reset the filing clock to the later of its October 21, 2021 action or Presbytery's October 20, 2020 ruling, it was filed more than 30 days later. The merits were not reached. An attached SJC response to CCB separately defended its record-reopening in Case 2020-12 and asked CCB to deny an exception request as untimely, waived, and procedural. complaint administratively out of order; dismissed not reached legacy 2022-1 43-3 administratively out of order untimely complaint BCO 43-3 thirty-day filing deadline complaint timing untimely filing BCO 43-3 timeliness complaint procedure"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2022-01</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga49_2022__2022-01.md">Eagle v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2021-11" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2021-11 Park et al. v. Korean Central Presbytery Teaching elders challenged Korean Central Presbytery’s summary censure of a minister before an indictment was prepared. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s action because discipline preceded particular charges and a specific confession, and because an independent church lacked authority to impose PCA censure. It declared the underlying matter moot because the alleged event was twenty-one years old and the victim would not cooperate, ending the proceeding without remand. The ruling addressed neither the allegations’ merits nor all old charges categorically. complaint sustained; remanded not stated legacy 2021-11 30-1 31-2 31-3 32-3 32-20 34-6 34-7 38-1 39-3 39-3.3 censure without indictment BCO 32-3 disciplinary procedure sexual misconduct pastor-congregant mootness non-PCA discipline teaching elder discipline BCO 38-1 without process statute of limitations BCO 32-20 cooperating victim"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2021-11</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga50_2023__2021-11.md">Park et al. v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2021-12" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2021-12 Michelson v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery The Michelsons’ complaint challenged a congregational meeting’s procedure for electing three assistant pastors as associate pastors—allegedly without a pulpit committee, ballots, counted abstentions, or protection for a substantial minority. The SJC dismissed it as not judicially in order: BCO 43-1 requires complaint against an act or decision of a court, but the complaint attacked congregational actions, while the Session’s only act was calling the meeting and was not objected to. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2020-13" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2020-13 Benyola v. Central Florida Presbytery The SJC dismissed Peter Benyola's complaint against Central Florida Presbytery as administratively out of order because he lacked standing to complain of the Presbytery's action. Benyola was neither a teaching elder member of that Presbytery nor a ruling elder commissioner representing a member church at the September 18, 2020 meeting when the Presbytery considered and denied the complaint. Citing prior SJC standing decisions, the Commission held the defect could not be cured and dismissed unanimously, 22-0-0, without reaching the merits. complaint administratively out of order; dismissed not reached legacy 2020-13 administratively out of order standing presbytery commissioner"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2020-13</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga48_2021__2020-13.md">Benyola v. Benyola was neither a teaching elder member of that Presbytery nor a ruling elder commissioner representing a member church at the September 18, 2020 meeting when the Presbytery considered and denied the complaint. <section class="judicial-year" data-judicial-year="2019"><h2>2019</h2><div class="judicial-year__records"><article class="judicial-case" id="case-2019-01" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2019-01 Dodson et al. v. Ohio Presbytery Grace PCA’s Session challenged Ohio Presbytery’s reversal of excommunication for two members convicted of heresy. The SJC partially sustained the complaint: prior indefinite suspension was not constitutionally required, but Presbytery properly found excommunication too severe because the trial record contained no evidence of contumacy. Presbytery nevertheless had to impose an appropriate lesser censure or remand for one, and lacked authority to mandate transfer to another church. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2019-03" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2019-03 Crouse v. Northwest Georgia Presbytery A serving deacon nominated for ruling elder complained that his session removed his nomination before BCO 24-1 instruction or examination. The SJC held the session erred by adding an unwritten pre-examination 'vetting' removal and that Northwest Georgia Presbytery erred in approving it: BCO 24-1's sequence—instruction and examination before the session determines eligibility—is mandatory. The ruling reserved the session's sound discretion and the treatment of frivolous or clearly disqualified nominees. The complaint was sustained and remanded for adjudication consistent with the decision.</p><div class="judicial-case__topics" aria-label="Topic tags"><span class="judicial-pill">officer nomination process</span><span class="judicial-pill">ruling elder election</span><span class="judicial-pill">session prescreening nominees</span><span class="judicial-pill judicial-pill--more">+3 topics</span></div><div class="judicial-case__footer"><a href="../cases/ga48_2021__2019-03.md">Read case <span aria-hidden="true">→</span></a><details class="judicial-details"><summary>Case details</summary><dl><div><dt>Matter type</dt><dd>Complaint</dd></div><div><dt>Final disposition</dt><dd>Sustained</dd></div><div><dt>Review basis</dt><dd>Great deference unless clear error (discretion and judgment)</dd></div><div><dt>BCO provisions</dt><dd>BCO 24-1, BCO 24-6, BCO 39-3, BCO 14-7, BCO 3-2, BCO 31-2, BCO 32-2, BCO 29-1, BCO 29-3, BCO 31-7, BCO 32-3, BCO 31-5, BCO 32-16, BCO 32-19, BCO 31-8, BCO 27-4, BCO 32-18, BCO 42-3, BCO 42-6, BCO 30-1, BCO 36-5, BCO 42-5, BCO 35-13, BCO 42-4, BCO 42-8, BCO 39-3.1, BCO 20-2</dd></div><div><dt>Aliases</dt><dd>legacy 2019-3</dd></div><div><dt>All topic tags</dt><dd>officer nomination process, ruling elder election, session prescreening nominees, mandatory sequence BCO 24-1, divorce and church office, session discretion</dd></div></dl></details></div></article>
<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2019-04" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2019-04 Williams v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2018-01" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2018-01 Glen Mapes v. Metropolitan New York Presbytery A ruling elder appealed convictions and censures arising from his brief refusal to leave a closed Temporary Session meeting. The SJC affirmed only his conviction for failing to submit to church government, because he knowingly attended and his apology acknowledged fault; it reversed findings of dereliction, sedition, rioting, and the balance for lack of supporting evidence. <section class="judicial-year" data-judicial-year="2017"><h2>2017</h2><div class="judicial-year__records"><article class="judicial-case" id="case-2017-01" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2017-01 Dailey v. Heritage Presbytery Heritage Presbytery treated a member's September 2016 filing against her session as a BCO 43-3 complaint and began adjudicating it. The SJC sustained RE Scott Dailey's complaint against that action. BCO 43-3 allows higher-court review only if the lower court denies a complaint or fails to consider it by its next stated meeting. The session timely ruled the filing did not meet BCO 43-1 and did consider it, so neither condition applied. The SJC sustained the appeal: Presbytery violated BCO 15-3 by dividing the verdict and amending the censure, which it had to approve or disapprove as a whole without debate. Bachmann's earlier procedural challenges were not sustained; his unconditional post-trial confession waived them. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2016-16" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2016-16 Sartorius v. Siouxlands Presbytery Did a presbytery fail in its duty to condemn erroneous opinions by acquitting a minister on theological-error charges? The SJC denied the complaint, leaving the acquittal undisturbed. A complaint against a not-guilty verdict cannot provoke a retrial at the superior court; under BCO 43 the superior court may only annul or remand, not reverse, and the complainant bore the burden to show error from the record. The record contained the defendant's testimony, including recantations or clarifications, Defense Exhibit 1, and witness testimony sufficient to refrain from contradicting the trial court. The SJC expressly did not decide the defendant's actual views. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2016-01" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2016-01 Aven v. Ohio Valley Presbytery An SJC complaint alleged that Ohio Valley Presbytery failed to comply with the SJC's prior remand in Case 2014-01, which required it to 'hear further' from TE Charles Hickey about his changed view on Larger Catechism 177. The SJC denied the complaint. It held that the prior decision neither sustained nor denied the original complaint and prescribed no particular examination procedure; Hickey's nine pages of additional affirmations, exegesis, and answers constituted hearing further, and he addressed the five identified areas at least in part. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2016-02" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2016-02 Robertstad v. Robertstad initially filed by e-mail—not an allowed filing—and his hard-copy filing arrived after the thirty-day deadline. The SJC reasoned that BCO 42-4/43-3 notification language concerns a lower court notifying parties, not party e-filing, and OMSJC 18.10.b bars e-mail filing. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2016-14" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2016-14 Wills v. Metro Atlanta Presbytery Did a presbytery violate the BCO or clearly err by dissolving a congregation without its consent? The SJC said no and denied the complaint. The denial left dissolution in place and warned that such action still requires sufficient justification and prudent, reviewable procedure.</p><div class="judicial-case__topics" aria-label="Topic tags"><span class="judicial-pill">dissolution of a church</span><span class="judicial-pill">presbytery power over congregations</span><span class="judicial-pill">BCO 13-9 presbytery powers</span><span class="judicial-pill judicial-pill--more">+5 topics</span></div><div class="judicial-case__footer"><a href="../cases/ga45_2017__2016-14.md">Read case <span aria-hidden="true">→</span></a><details class="judicial-details"><summary>Case details</summary><dl><div><dt>Matter type</dt><dd>Complaint</dd></div><div><dt>Final disposition</dt><dd>Denied</dd></div><div><dt>Review basis</dt><dd>Multiple review bases</dd></div><div><dt>BCO provisions</dt><dd>BCO 13-9, BCO 13-9.f, BCO 13-10, BCO 15-2, BCO 12-6, BCO 31-2, BCO 31-10, BCO 40-6, BCO 43-1, BCO 43-2, BCO 39-3, BCO 39-3.3, BCO 39-3.4, BCO 24-7, BCO 40-5, BCO 43-3, BCO 43-5, BCO 43-3.37</dd></div><div><dt>Aliases</dt><dd>legacy 2016-14</dd></div><div><dt>All topic tags</dt><dd>dissolution of a church, presbytery power over congregations, BCO 13-9 presbytery powers, BCO 40-6 process against lower courts, church dissolution without consent, complaint procedure, Grace North Atlanta Church, Metro Atlanta Presbytery</dd></div></dl></details></div></article>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2015-01" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2015-01 Sanfacon v. Philadelphia Presbytery The SJC held that a ruling elder’s complaint was administratively out of order and could not be put in order because the original complaint was filed 78 days after the challenged Session action—18 days beyond BCO 43-2’s 60-day window. A second complaint was merely an extension of the untimely first. Even though Session and Presbytery recognized the untimeliness but addressed it anyway, the SJC voided all lower-court actions on the complaints. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2013-10" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2013-10 Latimer v. Chicago Metro Presbytery A presbytery deposed a minister for violating his seventh vow by pursuing an unbiblical divorce after he filed a civil petition. The SJC sustained the appeal in part: the presbytery clearly erred in finding sin in the filing, because the record did not conclusively show intent to divorce rather than protect his children, and the wife's counter-filing undermined the failure-to-withdraw inference. The SJC rejected prejudice, irregularity, and venue claims, voided the trial judgment, and noted that his expired prior suspension left him a presbytery member without call. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2013-07" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2013-07 Session of First Presbyterian Church North Port v. Presbytery of Southwest Florida The SJC sustained the Session's complaint against Presbytery. Presbytery had ruled a member's original complaint administratively out of order as untimely but then remanded the matter to the Session; the SJC held that once out of order, no complaint remained to remand. It also held Presbytery could not direct or instruct the Session to initiate formal process without BCO 40-5's required citation step, so those directions were null and void. Presbytery had ruled a member's original complaint administratively out of order as untimely but then remanded the matter to the Session; the SJC held that once out of order, no complaint remained to remand. It also held Presbytery could not direct or instruct the Session to initiate formal process without BCO 40-5's required citation step, so those directions were null and void. The member remained under the Session's jurisdiction; the civil trespass order was not ecclesiastical discipline and did not alter membership.</p><div class="judicial-case__topics" aria-label="Topic tags"><span class="judicial-pill">complaint procedure</span><span class="judicial-pill">timeliness of complaint</span><span class="judicial-pill">civil trespass order</span><span class="judicial-pill judicial-pill--more">+13 topics</span></div><div class="judicial-case__footer"><a href="../cases/ga42_2014__2013-07.md">Read case <span aria-hidden="true">→</span></a><details class="judicial-details"><summary>Case details</summary><dl><div><dt>Matter type</dt><dd>Complaint</dd></div><div><dt>Final disposition</dt><dd>Sustained; Remanded</dd></div><div><dt>Review basis</dt><dd>Not stated</dd></div><div><dt>BCO provisions</dt><dd>BCO 40-4, BCO 40-5, BCO 43-1, BCO 43-2, BCO 43-3, BCO 43-8, BCO 43-9, BCO 43-10, BCO 11-4, BCO 31-1, BCO 40-6, BCO 43-6</dd></div><div><dt>Aliases</dt><dd>legacy 2013-7</dd></div><div><dt>All topic tags</dt><dd>complaint procedure, timeliness of complaint, civil trespass order, church member rights, presbytery jurisdiction, review and control, BCO 40-5 process, directing session to initiate process, membership standing, original jurisdiction, member discipline, session jurisdiction, presbytery authority over session, due process, excommunication without charges, BCO 40-4 remand</dd></div></dl></details></div></article>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2013-11" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2013-11 Session of First Presbyterian Church North Port, Florida v. Presbytery of Southwest Florida A Session appealed Presbytery’s judgment finding it guilty and suspending it for refusing instructions to institute process against a member. The SJC sustained the appeal, reversed the judgment in whole, and dismissed the charges. Once Presbytery denied the member’s complaint, that matter should have ended; moreover, Presbytery did not follow BCO 40-4’s required first step before invoking BCO 40-5 review and control. The delay, prejudice, and missing-witness specifications were moot. The decision did not fault Presbytery’s underlying concern. appeal sustained not stated legacy 2013-11 40-4 40-5 42-6 15-3 34-1 appeal civil trespass order church member rights presbytery jurisdiction review and control BCO 40-5 process trial by presbytery judicial commission suspension of session irregularities in proceedings double jeopardy prejudice of judge refusal of reasonable indulgence"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2013-11</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga42_2014__2013-11.md">Session of First Presbyterian Church North Port, Florida v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2011-11" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2011-11 Steven Hahn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery Hahn challenged Presbytery’s ruling that CTKPC Session lawfully excluded him from that congregation’s worship until a psychiatric evaluation addressed safety concerns. The SJC denied the complaint. Applying BCO 39-3.3, it found no clear error in the lower courts’ credibility and discretionary judgments, given Session’s familiarity with the people and events. It characterized the restriction as informal pastoral safety guidance, not judicial discipline: it did not bar sacraments, worship elsewhere, or transfer, and attendance could resume upon medical assurance. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2011-12" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2011-12 Steven Hahn v. Philadelphia Metro West Presbytery Hahn appealed Presbytery’s guilty judgment and indefinite suspension from the sacraments, alleging trial irregularities, denial of a requested amendment, haste, and prejudice. The SJC denied the appeal on all three charges: false and unsubstantiated accusations, disobedience and disrespect toward church authorities, and a bitter and malignant spirit. Applying BCO 39-3.3, it deferred to Presbytery’s familiarity with the parties, witnesses, and extensive trial record and found no clear error, even though contrary evidence may have existed. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2011-14" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2011-14 Reese and Bech v. Philadelphia Presbytery Philadelphia Presbytery declared Reese and Bech's complaint out of order because some supporting reasons and requested amends allegedly violated the BCO. The SJC sustained the complaint, holding Presbytery misapplied Robert's Rules: objectionable parts do not justify rejecting an entire complaint, and a court need not adopt requested amends. Ruff challenged Presbytery's failure to investigate a teaching elder, but BCO 43 requires a complaint against an act or decision; lack of action qualifies only when a court meeting has occurred and the court failed to act. Presbytery's nearest antecedent meeting was August 18, 2010, and Ruff filed October 27, 2010, beyond BCO 43-2's thirty-day limit. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2010-03" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2010-03 McNeil v. Chesapeake Presbytery An appellant under suspension from the sacraments challenged the presbytery's judicial commission process and censure. The SJC held the appeal judicially out of order—not decided on the merits—because he had not submitted to a regular trial, as BCO 42-2 requires. Treated as a complaint, it was also out of order: it had not first been presented to the presbytery, and the 30-day period had expired. The SJC further barred complaints about later court actions while he remained under censure, except as to the highest censure. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2010-16" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2010-16 Lyons v. Western Carolina Presbytery Kirk Lyons filed BCO 32-2 charges against TE Craig Bulkeley with Western Carolina Presbytery. WCP dismissed the charges, then ruled Lyons's complaint administratively out of order for lack of standing. The SJC answered that the dismissal was not erroneous—Presbytery had discretion under BCO 31-8, 34-2, and 32-20, and the record showed no clear error—but that WCP erred on standing because Lyons's filing brought him under its jurisdiction. WCP dismissed the charges, then ruled Lyons's complaint administratively out of order for lack of standing. The SJC answered that the dismissal was not erroneous—Presbytery had discretion under BCO 31-8, 34-2, and 32-20, and the record showed no clear error—but that WCP erred on standing because Lyons's filing brought him under its jurisdiction. Because that error was not prejudicial, the SJC denied the complaint.</p><div class="judicial-case__topics" aria-label="Topic tags"><span class="judicial-pill">standing to bring complaint</span><span class="judicial-pill">BCO 32-2 charges</span><span class="judicial-pill">BCO 31-8 disqualified accusers</span><span class="judicial-pill judicial-pill--more">+7 topics</span></div><div class="judicial-case__footer"><a href="../cases/ga39_2011__2010-16.md">Read case <span aria-hidden="true">→</span></a><details class="judicial-details"><summary>Case details</summary><dl><div><dt>Matter type</dt><dd>Complaint</dd></div><div><dt>Final disposition</dt><dd>Denied</dd></div><div><dt>Review basis</dt><dd>Great deference unless clear error (discretion and judgment)</dd></div><div><dt>BCO provisions</dt><dd>BCO 15-3, BCO 31-8, BCO 32-2, BCO 32-3, BCO 32-20, BCO 34-2, BCO 38-4, BCO 39-3, BCO 43-1, BCO 43-2</dd></div><div><dt>Aliases</dt><dd>legacy 2010-16</dd></div><div><dt>All topic tags</dt><dd>standing to bring complaint, BCO 32-2 charges, BCO 31-8 disqualified accusers, BCO 34-2 scandalous charges on slight grounds, BCO 32-20 one-year limitation, communing member in good standing, erasure from church roll, dismissal of charges, judicial commission authority, malignant spirit toward accused</dd></div></dl></details></div></article>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2009-21" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2009-21 Armes v. Southwest Florida Presbytery Armes challenged Presbytery's refusal to hear his second complaint about Session's trespass notice and threat of arrest, which Presbytery treated as duplicating his pending excommunication complaint. The SJC sustained the complaint because the trespass action occurred later and was distinct, although the matters could be heard together. It remanded for Presbytery or a commission to hear the complaint under BCO 43-8. The SJC did not decide whether Session could issue such a notice; review remained subject to timely filing and standing. complaint partially sustained; remanded not stated legacy 2009-21 38-1 43-1 43-2 43-4 43-8 30-4 excommunication standing to complain trespass notice complaint procedure remand same substance"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2009-21</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga39_2011__2009-12_2009-21.md">Armes v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2009-22" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2009-22 McNeil v. Chesapeake Presbytery The SJC denied a censured husband's complaint against Chesapeake Presbytery's approval of a judicial commission report, which had upheld his session's refusal to receive his charges against his wife after she filed for civil divorce. Applying BCO 39-3.2–3.3, the SJC deferred to the lower courts' factual and discretionary findings absent clear error. It found no clear procedural error, upheld the conclusion that the wife did not sin by seeking civil protection, and invoked BCO 31-8's caution about accusations from one under censure. complaint denied mixed legacy 2009-22 31-8 39-3.2 39-3.3 13-9 32-20 39-3 32-2 43-1 32-3 31-2 34-2 church discipline marital conflict charges against spouse great deference appellate review civil courts"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2009-22</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga39_2011__2009-22.md">McNeil v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2009-23" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2009-23 Koerkenmeier v. Illiana Presbytery Illiana Presbytery appointed a commission with broad power 'to deal with matters' at Center Grove Presbyterian Church after a pastor requested inquiry into alleged evils. The SJC sustained the complaint but held the error harmless: the broad charge could take original jurisdiction from the session contrary to BCO 11-3 &amp; 4 and 33-1, while a limited investigative committee under BCO 13-9(f) and 31-2 would have been proper. Because the commission never exercised that power and the session endorsed its findings, no remedy, including invalidation of the adopted report, was ordered. complaint sustained not stated legacy 2009-23 11-3 11-4 13-9 13-9.f 31-2 33-1 presbyterial oversight commission powers congregational jurisdiction original jurisdiction BCO 13-9f harmless error"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2009-23</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga39_2011__2009-23.md">Koerkenmeier v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2009-24" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2009-24 Phelps v. Pacific Presbytery Phelps complained that Pacific Presbytery erred by finding no constitutional irregularities in the New Life Burbank Session's ordination of Lee Irons as a ruling elder, despite PP's earlier refusal to receive Irons as a teaching-elder candidate. The SJC denied the complaint. Under BCO 39-3.3, the Court owed great deference to the lower court's discretionary fitness judgment; the single office of elder does not require identical eligibility processes, and the NLB Session had jurisdiction after Irons renounced OPC jurisdiction. PP's action stood; the SJC declined to decide the NAPARC issue. complaint denied discretion and judgment legacy 2009-24 8-9 18-3 21-4 21-5 24-1 24-6 39-3.3 ruling elder ordination teaching elder ordination OPC discipline one office two forms renunciation of jurisdiction NAPARC presbytery discretion"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2009-24</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga39_2011__2009-24.md">Phelps v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2009-25" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2009-25 Brown v. Northern California Presbytery Brown challenged Presbytery’s abstract approval of six views concerning diaconal practice. The SJC sustained the consolidated complaints and annulled Presbytery’s action because a church court cannot issue a binding decree apart from properly exercising jurisdiction over specific persons. Constitutional conformity must instead be determined through authorized examination or judicial processes. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2009-28" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2009-28 Ruff v. Nashville Presbytery Nashville Presbytery's BCO 31-2 investigation of reports against TE George Grant was inadequately documented and internally inconsistent, and the evidence before Presbytery raised a strong presumption of guilt, the SJC held. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2009-11" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2009-11 Larry Edison et al. v. Southwest Florida Presbytery Ministers complained that Southwest Florida Presbytery improperly reexamined Bryan Gregory and reversed his examination, membership, and call after previously receiving him. The SJC upheld Presbytery’s authority to hear and sustain the earlier complaint but sustained the present complaint on the remedial actions. Sustaining a complaint did not itself undo prior acts; once Presbytery had treated Gregory as a member, his membership rights could be removed only through disciplinary due process. The SJC annulled the reexamination and March 24 actions and directed Presbytery to consider appropriate remedies. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2008-14" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2008-14 White v. Siouxlands Presbytery A minister complained that his presbytery wrongly refused to order a BCO 31-2 investigation into another minister’s Covenant of Works/Federal Vision views. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded for that investigation, holding that BCO 31-2 requires investigation of credible, injurious reports about Christian character. The presbytery erred by applying the higher evidentiary standard for conviction after process; reports sufficient to trigger investigation need not establish guilt or a strong presumption of guilt, and hearsay or conflicting testimony can require investigation rather than justify refusal. A concurrence agreed in result; the dissent found no clear error in the presbytery’s exercise of discretion. complaint sustained; remanded not stated legacy 2008-14 31-2 31-5 31-7 31-8 32-2 35-1 35-3 39-3 39-3.3 39-3.4 40-4 40-5 8-2 BCO 31-2 investigation Federal Vision theology Covenant of Works presbytery oversight duty hearsay judicial investigation Westminster Standards appellate deference BCO 39-3 great discretion New Perspective on Paul"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2008-14</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga38_2010__2008-14.md">White v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2008-15" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2008-15 Morton Smith v. Western Carolina The complaint challenged Presbytery’s commissions and its response to a canceled congregational meeting. The SJC upheld the Inman Commission because a Session may reference limited duties without congregational consent. It sustained the challenges to Presbytery’s consideration of the August 7 meeting and appointment of the Sealy Commission because the Session majority had validly canceled the meeting. Linton’s and Pellom’s calls therefore remained undissolved and Neville was uncalled, absent later congregational action. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2008-18" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2008-18 Hutchinson &amp; Bulkeley v. Western Carolina Hutchinson and Bulkeley challenged Presbytery’s refusal to condemn RE Neill Payne’s views in a circulated “Africa e-mail.” The SJC did not sustain the complaint. It held that a presbytery may not condemn a church officer’s allegedly erroneous opinions without due process and that four sentences, an approving newspaper reference, and the Commission’s summary did not present Payne’s views fully enough for responsible adjudication. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2008-01" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2008-01 Session of Crossroads Community Church v. Philadelphia Presbytery Two consolidated complaints challenged Philadelphia Presbytery’s licensing and ordination of a candidate who believed Scripture could permit women to hold the deacon’s office but promised to follow the BCO and not ordain women. The SJC denied both complaints and affirmed Presbytery. It distinguished subscription to doctrinal standards from approval of BCO practices, applied a three-part inquiry, and deferred to Presbytery on the candidate’s credible vow. Because complainants identified no violated doctrinal standard, no error was shown. The ruling reaffirmed that the BCO bars ordaining women as deacons. complaint denied; affirmed discretion and judgment legacy 2008-1 7-2 9-3 21-4 39-3 ordination licensure women deacons stated difference confessional subscription"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2008-01</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga37_2009__2008-01_2008-10.md">Session of Crossroads Community Church v. Philadelphia Presbytery</a></h3></div><div class="judicial-actions"><button type="button" class="judicial-actions__button" aria-haspopup="menu" aria-expanded="false" aria-label="Actions for Session of Crossroads Community Church v. Philadelphia Presbytery">⋯</button><div class="judicial-actions__menu" role="menu" hidden><button type="button" role="menuitem" data-judicial-action="save">Save to bookshelf</button><button type="button" role="menuitem" data-judicial-action="cite">Copy citation</button><button type="button" role="menuitem" data-judicial-action="link">Copy link</button></div></div></header><p class="judicial-case__outcome"><span>Outcome</span> Denied; Affirmed</p><p class="judicial-case__summary">Two consolidated complaints challenged Philadelphia Presbytery’s licensing and ordination of a candidate who believed Scripture could permit women to hold the deacon’s office but promised to follow the BCO and not ordain women. The SJC denied both complaints and affirmed Presbytery. It distinguished subscription to doctrinal standards from approval of BCO practices, applied a three-part inquiry, and deferred to Presbytery on the candidate’s credible vow. Because complainants identified no violated doctrinal standard, no error was shown. The ruling reaffirmed that the BCO bars ordaining women as deacons.</p><div class="judicial-case__topics" aria-label="Topic tags"><span class="judicial-pill">ordination</span><span class="judicial-pill">licensure</span><span class="judicial-pill">women deacons</span><span class="judicial-pill judicial-pill--more">+2 topics</span></div><div class="judicial-case__footer"><a href="../cases/ga37_2009__2008-01_2008-10.md">Read case <span aria-hidden="true">→</span></a><details class="judicial-details"><summary>Case details</summary><dl><div><dt>Matter type</dt><dd>Complaint</dd></div><div><dt>Final disposition</dt><dd>Denied; Affirmed</dd></div><div><dt>Review basis</dt><dd>Great deference unless clear error (discretion and judgment)</dd></div><div><dt>BCO provisions</dt><dd>BCO 7-2, BCO 9-3, BCO 21-4, BCO 39-3</dd></div><div><dt>Aliases</dt><dd>legacy 2008-1</dd></div><div><dt>All topic tags</dt><dd>ordination, licensure, women deacons, stated difference, confessional subscription</dd></div></dl></details></div></article>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-2008-10" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2008-10 Mark Grasso et al. v. Philadelphia Presbytery The complaint challenged Presbytery’s approval of a candidate who believed women could hold the diaconal office but promised to follow the BCO, which permits only men to be ordained as deacons. The SJC denied the complaint and affirmed approval of his ordination examination. It held that a BCO difference is evaluated through compliance, doctrinal, and ordination-vow inquiries; the record supported compliance and a credible vow, while complainants had not identified violated doctrinal standards. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2008-09" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2008-09 Session of Red Mountain Presbyterian Church v. Evangel Presbytery Red Mountain Session challenged Presbytery’s ruling that it had inadequately addressed a member’s demand to declare his wife’s divorce unbiblical, and Presbytery’s resulting declaration and Matthew 18 instruction. The SJC sustained all four issues and reversed Presbytery. It held Session’s context-sensitive ruling disclosed no clear error, use of BCO 31-2 was reasonable, Presbytery violated BCO 15-3 by allowing its commission to revise a report after floor discussion, and Presbytery judged the wife without due process. The SJC expressly did not decide whether biblical divorce grounds existed. complaint sustained; reversed not stated legacy 2008-9 31-2 15-3"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2008-09</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga37_2009__2008-09.md">Session of Red Mountain Presbyterian Church v. The SJC sustained the complaint in part and vacated the judgment and censure: the commission had authority only to investigate, and Malone’s general acknowledgments neither confessed specific charges nor showed intent to waive process under BCO 38-1. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2007-13" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2007-13 David Kniseley et al. v. Rocky Mountain Presbytery On complaint from TE David Kniseley and others, the SJC reviewed Rocky Mountain Presbytery's refusal to forbid a mission church from giving an unordained female staff member the title 'Minister of Church Life.' The SJC denied the complaint. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2007-08" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2007-08 Jones v. Louisiana Louisiana Presbytery’s refusal to institute process after examining Steve Wilkins’s Federal Vision teachings was challenged for applying the wrong constitutional standard and overlooking a strong presumption that some views were out of conformity with the Westminster Standards. The SJC sustained the complaint and annulled Presbytery’s denial. A “difference” need not expressly contradict the Standards; Presbytery must independently investigate and classify it rather than accept the member’s assurance or shift the burden to objectors. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2003-04" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2003-04 Dr. and Mrs. Frank Chin v. James River Presbytery Ruling elders challenged James River Presbytery’s delay in honoring West End’s valid congregational vote to dissolve its pastoral relationship and a three-month salary gift to the pastor. The SJC held that Presbytery lacked a constitutional basis to delay the dissolution, but rejected the challenge to its benevolent use of its own civil funds. Complaints 16-01, 18-01, and 19-01 were judicially out of order; the others were in order. No remand or repayment was ordered. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2002-05" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2002-05 Plowman v. The chairman of Presbytery's Judicial Business Committee advised her that her appeal was out of order; Presbytery later ruled her complaint untimely. The SJC sustained her complaint: she had submitted to regular trial, making her appeal in order under BCO 42-2, and her complaint was timely after Presbytery's advice caused the appeal to be renamed. It remanded for Presbytery to adjudicate the appeal. Filing the appeal suspended the Lord's Table censure pending final adjudication; the SJC questioned the contumacy ruling. complaint sustained; remanded not stated legacy 2002-5 32-6.b 33-2 42-2 42-3 42-1 43-1 43-2 15-1 15-3 12-3 12-1 42-6 32-6 contumacy right of appeal submission to regular trial timely filing of complaint committee vs commission suspension from Lord's Table due process judicial business committee authority"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2002-05</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga32_2004__2002-05.md">Plowman v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2002-09" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2002-09 Merriam v. Tennessee Valley Presbytery The SJC denied TE Stuart H. It rejected procedural challenges—that the earlier called meeting was improperly convened and that TVP was prejudiced by prior cases—and found no clear error, applying BCO 39-3(2)'s deference to lower-court factual findings. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2002-16" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2002-16 Session of Delhi Presbyterian Church v. Louisiana Presbytery The SJC sustained a session's timely complaint that Louisiana Presbytery barred one of its members from the Lord's Table after assuming original jurisdiction. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction. The censure was therefore a nullity, and the member remained under his session. The SJC also held the jurisdictional assumption reviewable despite no timely complaint against it. Three commissioners dissented. original_jurisdiction_request sustained not_applicable legacy 2002-16 33-1 31-1 31-2 32-5 32-4 32-3 11-3 11-4 43-1 43-2 13-12 34-1 assumption of original jurisdiction BCO 33-1 refuses to act session jurisdiction over members presbytery jurisdiction contumacy Southern Poverty Law Center League of the South Steve Wilkins Auburn Avenue Presbyterian Church suspension from Lord's Table graded courts timely complaint constitutionality of presbytery action"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2002-16</code> <span>· Original-jurisdiction request</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga32_2004__2002-16.md">Session of Delhi Presbyterian Church v. Under BCO 33-1, a presbytery may assume jurisdiction only when the session 'refuses to act'; because the session had investigated and found no strong presumption of guilt, it acted, so LAP never acquired jurisdiction. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2002-01" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2002-01 Sang Bai Kim and RE Chan Soo Kim v. Korean Eastern Presbytery In a dispute arising from a Korean Eastern Presbytery congregational election, two ruling elders were tried, refused to plead, and were suspended from sacraments and office; KEP denied their appeal, then increased the censures to deposition and excommunication for contumacy. The SJC affirmed KEP's denial and the guilt findings, but reversed the increased censures. An appellate court may not increase a censure under BCO 42-9; the trial court retains discretion to remove or increase an indefinite suspension, though the appellate court may recommend a lesser censure. The original suspension remained. appeal sustained; affirmed; reversed not stated legacy 2002-1 10-4 29-1 30-3 32-3 32-6 37-3 39-3 41-3 42-9 Korean church appellate court authority increased censure on appeal excommunication deposition contumacy BCO 42-9 double jeopardy court of original jurisdiction cultural factors in Korean cases"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2002-01</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga31_2003__2002-01.md">Sang Bai Kim and RE Chan Soo Kim v. <section class="judicial-year" data-judicial-year="2001"><h2>2001</h2><div class="judicial-year__records"><article class="judicial-case" id="case-2001-34" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2001-34 Nichols and Couch v. James River Presbytery Church members challenged Presbytery’s repeated delay in granting a properly adopted congregational request to dissolve its pastoral relationship and its gift equivalent to three months of the pastor’s compensation. The SJC found seven complaints judicially out of order, sustained the dissolution-delay challenge, and rejected the gift challenge because Presbytery controlled its own civil property. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2001-01" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2001-01 Charles Kim v. Korean Capital Presbytery The SJC addressed whether a presbytery and its administrative/judicial commission could suspend a local session and assume original jurisdiction over charges against a ruling elder. It answered no: original jurisdiction belonged to the session, and a presbytery cannot &quot;act for&quot; a lower court by replacing congregationally elected elders. Preliminary Principle Six, BCO 16-2, and BCO 31-1/33-1 controlled; the commission's interpretation of BCO 13-9 conflicted with those principles. The Presbytery's and Commission's actions, including the censure approved by Presbytery, were reversed. appeal sustained; reversed not stated legacy 2001-1 13-9 appeal original jurisdiction Session censure church governance"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2001-01</code> <span>· Appeal</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga30_2002__2001-01.md">Charles Kim v. It answered no: original jurisdiction belonged to the session, and a presbytery cannot &quot;act for&quot; a lower court by replacing congregationally elected elders. Preliminary Principle Six, BCO 16-2, and BCO 31-1/33-1 controlled; the commission's interpretation of BCO 13-9 conflicted with those principles. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2001-06" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2001-06 Sang Bai Kim and RE Chan Soo Kim v. Korean Eastern Presbytery The SJC sustained a complaint by two ruling elders against Korean Eastern Presbytery over a disputed congregational meeting (three commissioners dissented). The session was deadlocked and had not called a requested meeting; KEP's administrative commission called and supervised the February 18, 2001 meeting, and KEP approved that action. The SJC reversed both lower-court actions, holding that BCO 25-2 places responsibility on the session and that the presbytery's proper course was to adjudicate a complaint under BCO 43, not act for the session. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2001-15" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2001-15 In Mo Chung v. Korean Capital Presbytery The SJC decided whether a presbytery and its special judicial commission could assume original jurisdiction over disciplinary charges against a church member. It sustained the appeal and reversed: the court of original jurisdiction for communicant members is the local church session. Because the appellant was a member of Korean Presbyterian Church of Washington, the presbytery and its commission acted contrary to constitutional standards when they adjudicated the charges and imposed excommunication. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2001-18" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2001-18 Sang Soo Ryoo v. Korean Capital Presbytery The SJC sustained an assistant pastor’s appeal from a three-year suspension from the sacraments after a Korean Capital Presbytery commission found him guilty of participating in the call of an allegedly unconstitutional presbytery meeting. The decisive defect was procedural: no indictment was served, no prosecutor was clearly appointed, and no trial minutes appeared in the record; service of an indictment with a witness list was critical. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2001-25" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2001-25 Anthony Dallison v. North Florida Presbytery After TE Anthony Dallison confessed spousal abuse and received an indefinite suspension, North Florida Presbytery later found him impenitent and deposed him and suspended him from the sacraments. Dallison complained that increasing the censure required fresh charges and trial. The SJC disagreed: his BCO 38-1 confession waived trial rights as to the original charge; the offender then had to satisfy the court of repentance, and the presbytery could investigate and impose higher censure under BCO 37-3, 37-4, 37-8, and 34-4b. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2001-28" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2001-28 Larry Ball v. Westminster Presbytery A complaint challenged Westminster Presbytery's denial of a challenge to its May 15, 2001 plan to withdraw from the PCA. The SJC answered no: the Presbytery did not err, and denied the complaint. BCO 25's local-church withdrawal right and the BCO Preface's grassroots principles extend to presbyteries unless expressly excluded, so a presbytery may determine its own membership and affiliation. The plan did not 'act for' local churches; they retained rights to remain in the PCA or leave, and retained property and internal operations. complaint not sustained; affirmed not stated legacy 2001-28 25-11 11-3 11-4 34-1 33-1 24-1 presbytery withdrawal ecclesiastical authority civil authority freedom of conscience Presbyterian governance structure grass-roots Presbyterianism property rights local church rights"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>2001-28</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga30_2002__2001-28.md">Larry Ball v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-2000-02" data-judicial-record data-search-text="2000-02 Adams v. Northeast Presbytery A prosecutor's complaint relating to Northeast Presbytery's judicial case was held administratively out of order by the SJC. The SJC adopted two grounds: BCO 43-1 bars a complaint about a matter subject to an appeal in another case, and the complaint sought retrial of an accused on charges of which he had been acquitted, relief the SJC could not grant. Although the related appeal was later withdrawn and the withdrawal approved, the SJC still applied BCO 43-1. A concurrence disputed that first ground and urged BCO clarification of appellate review of acquittals. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1998-01" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1998-01 Snapp v. James River Presbytery The complaint challenged James River Presbytery's approval of an ordination examination in which the candidate called the Genesis creation days God's anthropomorphic work days, not necessarily twenty-four-hour days. The complainant argued that view conflicted with WCF I.9. The SJC denied the complaint and answered 'No' to whether the Presbytery erred; the examination stood. It held the Presbytery had authority and discretion, no General Assembly had declared anthropomorphic days contrary to the Standards, and an advisory-committee study left the SJC unwilling to decide creation-day length. Shive v. Central Carolina Presbytery A church member appealed convictions and excommunication arising from vulgar statements to two patients, challenging the lack of pretrial reconciliation, recusals, the prosecutor’s participation in deliberations, and Presbytery procedure. The SJC left guilt intact and denied a new trial, though it held that a prosecutor may not deliberate as a judge. It reversed excommunication because the record did not show impenitence or contumacy, which could not be inferred from exercising the right to remain silent. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1997-02" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1997-02 Nickoley v. Rocky Mountain Rocky Mountain Presbytery cited Pastor Bruce Nickoley for contumacy during his trial, after he allegedly refused to tell his congregation to stop picketing, and immediately deposed him without a hearing. On appeal, the SJC sustained the appeal, holding the Presbytery misapplied BCO provisions on confession, citation, refusal to testify, and deposition; Nickoley neither confessed nor refused to appear. Although presbyteries have general authority to maintain order, serious charges require due process. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1997-06" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1997-06 Fitzsimmons v. Evangel Presbytery After a church member and deacon was excommunicated by his session, he appealed to Evangel Presbytery. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1997-16" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1997-16 Session, BPC, Concord, NC v. Central Carolina Presbytery (Complaint) The Session of Bible Presbyterian Church, Concord, complained that Central Carolina Presbytery wrongly accepted its moderator's ruling making RE Chris Dollar's interim Candidates Committee appointment &quot;null and void&quot; because Christ Covenant Session never approved it. The SJC answered both issues no and did not sustain the complaint, leaving Presbytery's action undisturbed. It reasoned that approval was conditional under CCP rules, the moderator expressed Presbytery's intention, Presbytery did not surrender jurisdiction, and BCO 39-3 required deference; it found no appearance of prejudice. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1993-01" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1993-01 Smith v. Northeast Presbytery Smith complained that Northeast Presbytery failed to provide pastoral care after dissolving Grace Presbyterian Church. The SJC rejected Presbytery's objections that the complaint lacked supporting reasons or was barred by Smith's protest, held it in order, but denied it on the merits. Distinguishing the pastoral 'power of order' from judicial 'power of jurisdiction,' the SJC ruled that the Constitution neither requires nor permits a presbytery to retain jurisdiction over individual members of a dissolved particular church, and that pastoral care of former members is generally discretionary; on these facts, Presbytery's efforts satisfied any duty. complaint denied not stated legacy 1993-1 3-2 3-4 5-2 5-3 11-1 11-4 25-12 31-1 43-3 45-5 dissolved congregation presbytery administrative commission church membership jurisdiction complaint procedure constitutional rights"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1993-01</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga22_1994__1993-01.md">Smith v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1993-02" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1993-02 Johnson v. The SJC rejected the licensure specifications because Presbytery had thoroughly examined repentance and doctrinal adherence, and no definitive PCA standard required exclusion on these facts. It sustained the pre-licensure supply issue under BCO 19-1, 22-5, and 22-6 and enjoined greater future circumspection. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1992-01" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1992-01 Smith v. Northeast Presbytery Smith challenged Northeast Presbytery’s ruling that his complaint was untimely and unconstitutional after it dissolved Grace Church and indefinitely postponed a proposed Braintree mission. The SJC sustained the complaint and remanded it for Presbytery adjudication. The May action first revealed Presbytery’s view that former members were outside the PCA, so the June complaint was timely. BCO 11-4 neither barred nor itself required care; responsibility arose here from the April referral to Presbytery’s missions committee. Care need not take the form of a mission, and mere dissolution alone would not create that responsibility. complaint sustained; remanded not stated legacy 1992-1 5-1 11-4 13-1 15-5 25-12 43-2 standing to complain membership after dissolution pastoral care of dissolved congregation presbytery jurisdiction remand"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1992-01</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga21_1993__1992-01.md">Smith v. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1992-02" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1992-02 Roberts v. New River Presbytery A congregation member complained that New River Presbytery erred in November 1991 by declining to accept TE Don Post Jr.'s resignation and dissolve his pastoral relation, instead appointing a commission. The SJC sustained the complaint. Under BCO 23-1, once the congregation concurred and no sufficient reasons to retain the pastor appeared, the resignation 'shall be accepted' and the relation dissolved; the Presbytery's general BCO 13-9 power did not override that specific provision. The Presbytery had already dissolved the relation on December 7, 1991; the adopted judgment ordered no remand. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1992-05" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1992-05 Parks et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery Complainants challenged a Session plan under which most elders voluntarily resigned, the Session granted severance and benefits to its former pastor, proposed about a year with an interim pastor before a permanent call, and contemplated revising local bylaws. The SJC denied all four items. It held that the BCO permitted jointly considered voluntary resignations, that severance concerned resignation and the budget rather than a pastoral call, and that the plan and bylaw proposal were not themselves unconstitutional. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1992-07" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1992-07 Conrad et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery (Case #2) A complaint arising from Central Carolina Presbytery’s refusal to prosecute TE Stephen O. Stout and to recognize his accusers as voluntary prosecutors was denied. The SJC framed two issues and answered both yes: the Presbytery could constitutionally adopt its Investigative Committee report and decline judicial process, because the Committee found no “strong presumption of guilt” under BCO 31-2; and it could refuse voluntary-prosecutor status, because BCO 31-1/31-3 left discipline to the Presbytery and made any voluntary prosecutor subject to its approval. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1991-05" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1991-05 Herman Gunter III et al. v. Central Florida Presbytery Two ruling-elder nominees challenged the Session’s refusal to approve them based on their theonomic views and perceived divisiveness. The full SJC denied the complaint, holding that the court of original jurisdiction may assess an unsettled theological position and whether it threatens the church’s peace, purity, or progress; divisiveness was therefore properly considered. The SJC sustained the complaint: ordination is perpetual, deposition requires judicial process, and rescission was out of order after implementation; Presbytery likewise could not suspend a local elder without due process. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1988-06" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1988-06 TE John T. DeBardeleben v. Philadelphia Presbytery A complaint challenged Philadelphia Presbytery’s approval of proceedings that cleared teaching and ruling elders without properly trying serious public accusations arising from Christ Church’s division. All three specifications were sustained because plea bargaining, dropped charges, and failure to hear necessary witnesses left the accusations unresolved. Presbytery’s action was annulled and de novo trials produced mixed convictions and acquittals. Harold Burkhart received six months’ suspension, Douglas McCready an admonition, and six former ruling elders three-month suspensions. The uneven-discipline claim was neither sustained nor denied because the evidence was insufficient; it too was remanded for investigation and necessary action.</p><div class="judicial-case__topics" aria-label="Topic tags"><span class="judicial-pill">complaint</span><span class="judicial-pill">referral to commission</span><span class="judicial-pill">Mississippi Valley Presbytery</span></div><div class="judicial-case__footer"><a href="../cases/ga16_1988__case1.md">Read case <span aria-hidden="true">→</span></a><details class="judicial-details"><summary>Case details</summary><dl><div><dt>Matter type</dt><dd>Complaint</dd></div><div><dt>Final disposition</dt><dd>Partially Sustained; Remanded</dd></div><div><dt>Review basis</dt><dd>Not stated</dd></div><div><dt>BCO provisions</dt><dd>None listed</dd></div><div><dt>Aliases</dt><dd>legacy 1988-2; Minutes 2</dd></div><div><dt>All topic tags</dt><dd>complaint, referral to commission, Mississippi Valley Presbytery</dd></div></dl></details></div></article>

<article class="judicial-case" id="case-1986-02" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1986-02 Vaughn E. Hathaway, Jr. et al. v. Grace Presbytery A complaint challenged Grace Presbytery's approval and installation of a candidate who had been divorced for his own infidelity and had remarried; the complainants argued Scripture, the Westminster Confession, BCO 16-3, and the Seventh General Assembly's divorce report barred ordination. The Judicial Commission did not sustain any of the four specifications and upheld Presbytery's action. Its adopted reason was that the PCA's constitutional statements do not explicitly address divorce and remarriage for church officers; noting wide interpretive disagreement, it called for study. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1986-03" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1986-03 Henry D. Knight, Jr. v. Palmetto Presbytery A ruling elder challenged Palmetto Presbytery’s publication, as an appendix to meeting minutes, of a letter never discussed at that meeting, and its handling of his complaint. The Judicial Commission sustained specifications 1 and 3: Presbytery had not clearly declared the publication erroneous, and it risked harming Covenant’s Session. Specifications 2 and 4 failed because Presbytery timely referred the complaint, though its record was inaccurate, and acted in good faith. Wuckovich v. Central Carolina Presbytery A ruling elder complained that Central Carolina Presbytery violated the BCO in examining and approving Rick Downs for ordination, citing five specifications about the call, Downs’s Sabbath exception, the revote after an initial disapproval, lack of Scriptural search, and ordination questions. The judicial commission held points 1, 2, 4, and 5 not sustained 11–0 and point 3 not sustained 10–1; the general complaint was not sustained 11–0, and the lower court decision was confirmed. Its explanatory opinion said the commission disagreed on the Sabbath/subscription question and acted largely because the specifications did not substantiate the complaint. complaint not sustained; affirmed not stated legacy 1984-1; Minutes 12-80 complaint presbytery action judicial commission appointed"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1984-01</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga12_1984__case1.md">Elder Roy J. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1984-02" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1984-02 Russell D. Toms and TE William L. Thompson v. Central Florida Presbytery Central Florida Presbytery received a minister while he had a pending call to labor in another presbytery. A Judicial Commission sustained the specification of error, holding that BCO 13-2,5 barred receiving him under those circumstances; the vote was 9–4. It also voted 13–0 to remand the entire matter for proper procedures regarding his admission to the PCA. The Commission commended the presbytery's aim of receiving him but ruled the process erroneous, leaving the admission to be handled through proper procedures. complaint sustained; remanded not stated legacy 1984-2; Minutes 12-81 13-2 complaint presbytery action judicial commission appointed"><header class="judicial-case__header"><div><p class="judicial-case__docket"><code>1984-02</code> <span>· Complaint</span><span class="judicial-saved-state" data-judicial-saved hidden> · Saved</span></p><h3><a href="../cases/ga12_1984__case2.md">Russell D. The complaint alleged Presbytery failed to take BCO 34-7 action and improperly reduced the charges. The Commission sustained both items and remanded for a new trial, reasoning that the confessed sins were not considered and the censure was not commensurate with the offenses charged; it did not itself convict or sentence him. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1983-02" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1983-02 Val H. Barleman et al. v. Presbytery of Ascension The General Assembly sustained a complaint against Ascension Presbytery for sustaining a candidate's ordination trials despite exceptions to PCA constitutional standards. The Commission upheld specifications that his Lord's Supper and baptism views denied required visible-church membership and that his women-deacons view conflicted with the BCO; it rejected specifications on Sabbath recreation and immersion. The Assembly annulled the Presbytery's sustaining action, but not the ordination itself, so the candidate remained on the roll. <article class="judicial-case" id="case-1983-08" data-judicial-record data-search-text="1983-08 Jack Eubanks et al. v. Central Carolina Presbytery Complainants challenged Presbytery’s called meeting and its actions concerning a judicial commission and church membership. The adopted adjudication sustained the objection to dissolving the commission by a 14–12 vote because Robert’s Rules required a two-thirds vote, and sustained without stated grounds the objection to ordering the dissolved commission to reassemble and revote. It rejected the challenges to the called meeting, Presbytery’s membership action, and its consideration of David Alexander’s complaint; the membership claim failed because church membership is not itself a court. The dismissal therefore reflected correction of the defect, not approval of proceeding without a quorum.</p><div class="judicial-case__topics" aria-label="Topic tags"><span class="judicial-pill">quorum requirement</span><span class="judicial-pill">presbytery competence</span><span class="judicial-pill">constitutional violation</span><span class="judicial-pill judicial-pill--more">+2 topics</span></div><div class="judicial-case__footer"><a href="../cases/ga03_1975__case1.md">Read case <span aria-hidden="true">→</span></a><details class="judicial-details"><summary>Case details</summary><dl><div><dt>Matter type</dt><dd>Complaint</dd></div><div><dt>Final disposition</dt><dd>Dismissed</dd></div><div><dt>Review basis</dt><dd>Not reached</dd></div><div><dt>BCO provisions</dt><dd>BCO 14-4</dd></div><div><dt>Aliases</dt><dd>legacy 1975-1; Minutes 3-12</dd></div><div><dt>All topic tags</dt><dd>quorum requirement, presbytery competence, constitutional violation, judicial complaint, ratification of actions</dd></div></dl></details></div></article></div></section>
